overview: Covers acute traumatic wound management at Role 1 in prolonged field care (PFC), after TCCC, when evacuation is delayed. It covers the basics a Role 1 provider can do in an austere setting: analgesia, irrigation, debridement, dressings, closure, and preventing and treating infection, using a Best / Better / Minimum format. Start telemedicine early and send photos of the wound.

keyPoints.text: Wound care hurts, so plan analgesia first. Best: a regional nerve block (only if fully trained and equipped) and/or a ketamine drip with midazolam pushes. Better: local anesthetic and/or a ketamine drip. Minimum: local anesthetic and/or any pain medication.
For smaller wounds, inject lidocaine into the wound margins and respect the maximum dose. The limit is higher when the lidocaine contains epinephrine.
keyPoints.quote: The maximum dose of lidocaine WITHOUT epinephrine is 3mg/kg (1% lidocaine has 10mg/mL and 2% lidocaine has 20mg/mL).

keyPoints.text: Irrigate as early as possible ('the solution to pollution is dilution'). Best: Dakin's solution or sterile isotonic fluid. Better: clean, potable tap water. Minimum: the cleanest water available, boiled and cooled if it is not potable.
keyPoints.quote: nonpotable water should be boiled for a minimum of 3 minutes and then cooled to body temperature

keyPoints.text: Match irrigation volume to wound size and contamination. Iodine, bacitracin or alcohol additives do not reduce infection, and very high pressure can damage tissue.
keyPoints.quote: 1–3L for small or clean wounds, 4–8L for intermediate or dirty wounds, and ≥9L for large or very dirty wounds.

keyPoints.text: Debride clearly dead tissue and keep tissue you are unsure about. Judge muscle by color, contraction, consistency and circulation. When unable to evacuate and serial debridement is impossible (Minimum/ICRC method), remove all nonviable and questionable tissue at once.
keyPoints.quote: tissue of uncertain viability should be preserved and re-examined in 24–48 hours

keyPoints.text: Plan hemorrhage control before debriding. For large extremity debridement, elevate the limb and place a tourniquet first; monitor tourniquet time closely and try to keep the total under 90 minutes. Use direct pressure with a hemostatic dressing for minor bleeding, and be ready to transfuse.
keyPoints.quote: Monitor the tourniquet times closely and attempt to keep the total tourniquet time <90 minutes.

keyPoints.text: Deep or large open wounds. Best: negative pressure wound therapy (commercial or field-expedient wound VAC). Better: wet-to-dry dressings, changed regularly. Minimum: a bulky dry dressing left in place if the wound stays clean.
keyPoints.quote: leave in place 4–7 days if wound is clean and without sign of infection

keyPoints.text: Most war wounds should be closed at a surgical facility. Do not primarily close puncture wounds or wounds with tissue loss. A laceration can be closed primarily only if it is clean, under little tension, and within the time window. When in doubt, leave the wound open.
keyPoints.quote: there has been <12 hours from injury to closure (this can be extended to 24 hours for lacerations to the face or scalp)

keyPoints.text: Give antibiotics as a complement to debridement and irrigation. In general, cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours for 24 hours is adequate for most dirty wounds; oral moxifloxacin or clindamycin, or IV ertapenem, are alternatives. Give tetanus prophylaxis based on the wound and the patient's immunization history (Appendix E).
keyPoints.quote: cefazolin 2g in 250 mL NS IV over 5 min every 8 hours for 24 hours is adequate for most dirty wounds

keyPoints.text: If a wound shows infection (more pain, redness, pus) or the patient becomes systemically ill: remove the dressings, reopen any closed wound, re-debride, change dressings more often and continue antibiotics. For severe infection, evacuate; if you cannot, get a telemedicine consult. If possible, switch to a different antibiotic from the one used for prevention.
keyPoints.quote: Continue antibiotics for 7–10 days, moxifloxacin 400mg PO daily, levofloxacin 750mg PO daily

watchFor: Debriding large wounds causes significant blood loss. Do not debride more than you can control with direct pressure or a tourniquet, and watch closely for bleeding afterward.
Use epinephrine-containing local anesthetic with caution in the tip of the nose, ears, penis, fingers and toes because of the risk of ischemia.
Closing a wound greatly increases the risk of infection. Close only wounds that are very clean and well debrided.
Do not probe chest wounds; debride them minimally to avoid creating a pneumothorax.
Complex wounds are best managed with a telemedicine consult. Send photos or video.
editionNotes: The Appendix G summary table (p. 24) limits tetanus prophylaxis to patients whose immunization status is unknown, while the body text (p. 10) and Appendix E (p. 21) base it on both the wound and the immunization history.
The stated Dakin's solution concentration, the 'half-strength' recipe and the instruction to dilute the mixed solution further (p. 4) are hard to reconcile. Confirm before mixing.
The sodium bicarbonate concentration in the Dakin's recipe (p. 4) differs from the one in the packing list (p. 22).
The body text (p. 4) lists Dakin's solution as a Best irrigant, while the summary table (p. 23) specifies dilute Dakin's solution.
